taxonomyNote: NatureServe lists it as Red-bellied Mudsnake.
fieldMarks: Non-venomous; adults 91-122 cm total length, females thicker-bodied, males longer-tailed.
Shiny blue-gray to black back, often with a metallic sheen.
Sides with salmon, pink or red bars; belly checkered with alternating red and black bars.
Flat head, slightly constricted neck and small inconspicuous eyes; smooth scales in 19 rows at midbody.
Juveniles similar but with a needle-like tail that adults lack.
behavior: Semiaquatic and fossorial; prowls in the open at night, buried in mud much of the time on land.
Eats sirens, amphiumas, other salamanders, frogs, tadpoles and fish.
Active March-November in Texas; hibernates in the northern part of its range and is active year-round in the south.
Lays 6-104 eggs (usually under 50), mostly July to early August.
habitat: Marshes, swampy lake margins, river-edge wetlands, oxbows, beaver ponds, slow mud-bottomed streams, sloughs, floodplains, ditches and brackish tidal areas; burrows in soft soil and wet debris.
range: Coastal Plain from southeastern Virginia to southern Florida, west to eastern Texas and north in the Mississippi Valley to southern Illinois. Not in Canada.
